dataset.input: An employee has been employed continuously for four years. The employer terminates the employment without giving any reason and without notice, stating that the employee's services are no longer required. The employee receives no payment in lieu of notice. What are the employee's rights under Nigerian labour law?
dataset.target: Under section 11(1) of the Labour Act, a contract of employment can be terminated by either party giving notice. Section 11(3) provides that where the contract has lasted more than three years, the minimum notice period is one month. Since the employer terminated without notice or payment in lieu, the employee is entitled to: (a) payment in lieu of notice equivalent to one month's wages, and (b) any accrued but unpaid entitlements. Additionally, under section 11(6), the employee may be entitled to damages for wrongful dismissal if the termination was not in accordance with the contract or Act. The employee should file a complaint at the National Industrial Court of Nigeria.

dataset.input: A female employee has worked for a company for 18 months. She becomes pregnant and informs her employer. The employer dismisses her two weeks later, stating that her performance was unsatisfactory. She had never received any prior warning or performance review. Is the dismissal lawful?
dataset.target: No. Under section 54(1) of the Labour Act, it is unlawful for an employer to terminate the contract of employment of a female employee by reason of her pregnancy or any reason connected with her pregnancy. The dismissal two weeks after notification of pregnancy creates a presumption that the dismissal is connected to the pregnancy, especially given the absence of prior warnings or performance issues. The employee may also have constitutional protection under section 42 of the Constitution (freedom from discrimination). Additionally, the Labour Act provides for maternity leave of 12 weeks on full pay (section 54(3)). The employee is entitled to reinstatement or damages. The proper forum is the National Industrial Court.
dataset.source: Labour Act, ss. 54(1), (3); Constitution of Nigeria 1999, s. 42

dataset.input: An employer wishes to recruit foreign nationals for specialized technical roles. What requirement under Nigerian immigration and labour law must the employer satisfy before employing a foreign national?
dataset.target: Under the Immigration Act and the Labour Act, an employer must (a) obtain a business permit from the Ministry of Interior authorizing the employer to engage expatriate staff, and (b) obtain a Combined Expatriate Residence Permit and Alien Card (CERPAC) and a Subject to Regularization (STR) visa for each foreign employee. Additionally, where the role requires professional qualifications, the employer must ensure the foreign national's qualifications are verified by the relevant professional body. Under the Labour Act, the employer must also register the contract of employment with the Ministry of Labour. The Employment Visa and Expatriate Quota system regulated by the Ministry of Interior governs all expatriate employment.
